claims.statement: A Scope is the ownership and isolation unit of PowerContext, identified by an opaque scope_id; resolving or selecting a Scope does not authenticate the caller or grant any permission.

ACCESS_MODE defaults to disabled; in disabled mode the server factory refuses to load an injected Access Control service or Authentication Provider, and per-operation authorization dependencies skip checks when no Access Control service is present.

In enforced mode the Server selects the Authentication Provider in this order: an injected Authentication Provider, then the identities file (multi-identity bearer), then the legacy auth.token (static bearer); if none is configured, startup raises MissingAuthenticationProviderError, so enforced mode never runs without a provider.

Settings validation couples the access modes: auth.enabled forces enforced mode, an identities file requires enforced mode and cannot be combined with a legacy token, a legacy token cannot be used with disabled mode, an enabled Dashboard in enforced mode requires a token, and a non-loopback bind without authentication is rejected unless explicitly allowed.

The legacy AUTH_TOKEN maps every valid bearer credential, compared in constant time, to one fixed service Principal server-token; that Principal is bootstrapped as a server observer and server administrator and becomes the static Scope preset, so the token identifies one administrator rather than individual users.

The multi-identity bearer provider loads a JSON identity file whose entries hold a credential_id, a SHA-256 token_digest, and a subject Principal; it rejects symbolic links and non-regular files, rejects group or other permission bits on POSIX, requires unique credential IDs and digests, rereads the file on each request, reports unavailability when the file becomes unreadable, and grants no implicit role.

AuthenticationResult is an immutable identity value: its subject and actor must be PrincipalRef values, it carries at most 100 unique subject groups that cannot collide with the subject or actor, and any credential_id is trimmed and at most 255 characters.

AuthenticationMiddleware authenticates every protected external HTTP request before routing: a rejected credential returns 401 unauthorized with a Bearer challenge, an unavailable or raising provider returns 503 authentication_unavailable, and a successful result is bound to the request for its handler.

The public access permission catalog consists of server.observe, server.admin, scope.read, scope.contribute, scope.review, scope.delegate, scope.admin, artifact.read, artifact.write, artifact.share, handoff.evidence.inspect, handoff.acknowledge and prompt.use; access.self is an internal authentication-only requirement excluded from the public set.

Access roles are a fixed set of twelve: handoff.viewer, handoff.receiver, artifact.viewer, prompt.user, artifact.owner, scope.viewer, scope.contributor, scope.reviewer, scope.delegator, scope.admin, server.observer and server.admin.

Each role maps to a fixed action set: scope.contributor carries scope.read and scope.contribute, scope.reviewer carries scope.read and scope.review, and scope.admin carries only scope.admin on the resource itself, while Scope roles imply child actions on Artifacts inside their Scope (for example scope.admin implies only artifact.share, and scope.viewer, scope.reviewer and scope.delegator imply artifact.read, handoff.evidence.inspect and prompt.use), so administration roles do not become content roles.

The built-in provider decides from one consistent snapshot of the policy revision, active bindings, Artifact owners and owned resources; a binding is active only while its state is active and it has not expired at the evaluation time, and when no binding grants the action an Artifact owner whose Principal matches the caller receives the artifact.owner actions, otherwise the decision is denied with no-matching-binding.

When the repository cannot provide one consistent snapshot, the decision reader retries the revision check up to three times and then fails closed with policy-snapshot-unstable; list operations derive their authorized resource filter from the same derivation as point decisions so the two cannot drift.

Every authorization decision except access.self is recorded in the audit store; denied decisions raise AccessDeniedError and an unavailable provider raises AccessUnavailableError, which the server maps to 403 forbidden, 401 when no Principal is present, and 503 respectively.

Each operation's access requirement is enforced by a per-route authorization dependency that resolves static, request-derived or named-resolver requirements into concrete (action, resource) checks and runs them before the handler, and the server maps a denied check of the static preset to a bootstrap-and-retry path.

The static Scope preset grants the static bearer Principal the five Scope roles scope.viewer, scope.contributor, scope.reviewer, scope.delegator and scope.admin on a Scope when the Scope is created or when a denied check comes from the preset; each grant is protected by a receipt key so a revoked grant is not recreated.
POST /v1/scopes requires server.admin on the Server resource, and creating a Prompt Artifact requires scope.admin on the target Scope while creating any other Artifact requires scope.contribute.

Reading an exact Scope selection checks scope.read on each named Scope, an all-Scope or subtree selection checks server.observe on the Server, and handoff continuation checks artifact.read and handoff.evidence.inspect while acknowledging an exact handoff revision checks handoff.acknowledge.

Scope binding resolution tries an explicit Scope ID first, then each durable binding key in order, and finally the default Scope pointer; the first existing binding decides and resolution does not fall through when its target is missing.

A missing explicit Scope or an absent binding and default yields 404 scope_not_found, while a binding or default pointer whose target Scope is missing yields 409 scope_binding_target_missing with the original target ID in error details, so clients must not silently create a replacement Scope.

The Scope service bootstraps a Default Scope with a fixed idempotency key and sets it as the default pointer, and reusing a Scope creation idempotency key with different parameters returns 409 scope_idempotency_conflict.

The built-in relational authorization provider is the one the server composes in enforced mode when no Access Control service is injected; it supports safe resource filtering, multi-requirement checks and relationship management, and opens the Access tables in the configured SQLite, OceanBase or SeekDB database.

The embedded Casbin adapter evaluates active bindings with a fresh Casbin enforcer and a fixed request and policy matcher, applies the same artifact owner rule as the built-in provider, and is opened only through open_casbin_access_control, which the server factory does not select.

The AuthZen adapter is decision-only: it posts to the AuthZen evaluation or evaluations endpoints, maps only the boolean decision and an optional bounded policy_revision into authzen-allow or authzen-deny, provides no relationship management, and refuses resource filtering with safe_resource_filtering_unavailable so list operations fail closed.

GET /v1/access/me reports the active access mode, the resource kinds, the Artifact families with their share units, and the provider capabilities (safe resource filtering, multi-requirement check, relationship management, group subjects, multi-principal and the direct resource key limit).

When an Artifact or Candidate owner write cannot share the business transaction, the server stages an ownership intent in pc_access_owner_recovery in the primary database during the domain commit, and delivers it before the response, so a delivery failure propagates to the caller and leaves the intent pending.

Owner recovery replay completes an accepted intent using only its persisted payload, writes the relation with the same owner and key, never accepts a caller-supplied owner, and a background monitor retries pending intents every five seconds in pages of 100 while skipping intents that fail.

Artifact owner recovery requires an audit store implementing append_audit_once, the idempotent capability that rejects a reused event ID with different fields, and the operation fails before the domain commit when that capability is missing.

Owner gap inventory returns bounded identity metadata with reasons unknown, pending, delivered_relation_missing or legacy_selector_required, never returns Artifact or Candidate bodies, and grants no ownership; no public HTTP, MCP or CLI endpoint exposes recovery operations.

Migrating legacy data after enabling enforced mode is explicit: artifacts and candidates created while Access was disabled stay read-only without an owner, the plan and apply routes require server.admin in enforced mode, apply names the owner for the call and refuses to run outside enforced mode, and existing relations are never modified.
The Dashboard supports only the built-in static bearer profile: the factory refuses to combine an enabled Dashboard with an injected Authentication Provider or Access Control service.
server/access.py performs transport access logging only and makes no authorization decision.

tests/test_access_control.py covers administration roles that do not become content writers, group bindings inherited from the trusted authentication context, cursors bound to policy revision and group membership, immutable and independent Artifact owners, Candidate owner locking, and built-in versus Casbin owner-rule parity.
